name: Hesperidin

lead: Hesperidin is a flavonoid concentrated in citrus peel, sold as a supplement and often paired with diosmin or vitamin C. People take it hoping to improve circulation around the eyes and reduce dark circles and puffiness.

It is thought to support vein and capillary tone and reduce leakage from small vessels, which would mean less blood pooling under thin eye skin. Clinical research on it concerns venous complaints such as those in the legs, and no trial in the sources reviewed has looked at under-eye appearance.

paras: It is taken as a daily capsule, usually alone or in a vein-support blend with diosmin, and sometimes appears in creams. Venous studies run for weeks to months, so any change would build gradually.

It is generally well tolerated; mild stomach upset, headache or rash are occasionally reported. It is recognised as safe as a food ingredient, but interactions with some liver-metabolised medications are possible.

angle.text: Users take hesperidin to support vein and capillary tone, so less blood pools under the eyes and dark circles and puffiness fade. It has been studied for venous and capillary complaints in the legs rather than under-eye appearance.

lead: Hesperidin is a flavanone glycoside found in citrus fruits, concentrated in the white inner peel; its aglycone is hesperetin.[1] It was first isolated in 1828 by the French chemist M. Lebreton.[1] It is sold as a dietary supplement, often combined with diosmin or vitamin C, in products aimed at venous and capillary complaints.[2][3]

In appearance communities it is discussed in the context of puffiness and dark circles, based on the idea that it supports small blood vessels. The sources reviewed contain no trial of hesperidin for periorbital puffiness or dark circles; the clinical literature concerns venous, metabolic and other conditions, and Wikipedia describes research on hesperidin as preliminary, with reviews finding no clear effect on blood lipids or blood pressure and inconclusive results on endothelial function.[1]

paras: Hesperidin and related citrus flavonoids are used in supplements for chronic venous insufficiency, haemorrhoids and capillary fragility, often in combination with diosmin.[2] A US over-the-counter label for a bruising product lists hesperidin methyl chalcone among citrus bioflavonoid ingredients alongside vitamin C, zinc, arnica and bromelain.[4] Its use for facial puffiness or under-eye circles is promoted in some products and discussions but has not been tested in published trials found in the sources reviewed.

Laboratory and animal work describes antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity for hesperidin and hesperetin, including activation of the Nrf2 pathway.[5][6] Authors have proposed effects on capillary permeability and endothelial function, but human evidence is limited.[1][6]

Hesperidin is poorly soluble and is largely absorbed as hesperetin after gut bacteria remove the sugar moiety. Human bioavailability of hesperidin and the related flavanone narirutin has been measured after orange juice ingestion.[7] A registered study compared the bioavailability of three hesperidin extracts.[8]

Reviews note no signs of toxicity at normal intakes of hesperidin and related compounds.[6] Mild gastrointestinal effects, headache and rash are occasionally reported with supplements in general; trials in the sources reviewed did not focus on adverse effects.
No studies found on hesperidin for facial puffiness, dark circles or other cosmetic outcomes.

Related research in other conditions: a 12-week open-label randomized trial in 98 people with metabolic syndrome compared hesperidin, flaxseed and their combination;[9] a controlled trial examined sulodexide and phlebotonic drugs in venous ulcers;[10] older European trials examined micronised flavonoid fractions in venous disease and in upper-limb lymphoedema after breast cancer treatment.[11][12] Systematic reviews of polyphenols include hesperidin among agents studied in rheumatoid arthritis.[13] A review of citrus flavonoids describes much of the evidence as epidemiological or preclinical.[3] Registered trials examine hesperidin for cognition, bone health in postmenopausal women, COVID-19 symptoms and metabolic syndrome.[14][15][16][17]
